source.title: ScaLA: Accelerating Adaptation of Pre-Trained Transformer-Based Language Models via Efficient Large-Batch Adversarial Noise
source.authors: Min-Jia Zhang; Niranjan Uma Naresh; Yu-Xiong He

record.file_problem: Text contains the full paper and appendix; some tables are flattened, so only clearly attributable values are recorded.
record.tranche_reason: Reports its own large-batch adaptation results and challenges a blanket claim that larger batches necessarily worsen held-out performance; it also evaluates whether adversarial noise changes that outcome.
record.gate_note: Tests large-batch adaptation, an adversarial-noise intervention, and Hessian sharpness on pretrained Transformers. Large-batch accuracy comparisons bear on V5; sharpness comparisons bear on the relation between sharpness and generalization, but not the magnitude-aware perturbation measure in V7. The study does not test random-label memorization, width, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, adaptive optimizer generalization generally, dropout, or removal of memorized examples. Values cited from prior work are not rows. Figures 1, 6, 7, and 8 are described in text but their individual values are not recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: Tests V5 in a new setting: downstream adaptation of pretrained Transformers. Six-epoch comparisons show a large-batch accuracy penalty and test whether recipe changes recover small-batch performance. Hessian measurements do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that ScaLA accelerates pretrained Transformer adaptation, matches or improves average small-batch performance, and outperforms tested large-batch methods. They interpret reduced Hessian curvature as explaining improved generalization; the experiments do not establish this explanation causally or test V7.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates pretrained BERTbase and RoBERTalarge adaptation to GLUE with large batches and adversarial embedding noise; versions concern natural-label generalization and batch-size effects, but the paper's intervention is ScaLA and its metric is task accuracy rather than train-test error gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, task, model, learning-rate choice, delayed versus immediate adversarial-noise injection, PGA perturbation steps, and use of groupwise learning rates affect reported outcomes. Figure 7 says accuracy tends to drop as batch size increases; ScaLA mitigates the gap.

fits_no_version.finding: The untreated large-batch model has a 2.6-fold larger largest Hessian eigenvalue than the small-batch model; ScaLA reduces it 6.9-fold relative to untreated large-batch adaptation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In pretrained BERT adaptation to MNLI, large batches increase Hessian curvature, and adversarial regularization reduces curvature alongside improved validation accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing adversarial noise lowers the method's reported average score from 89.4 to 88.6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial embedding regularization improves held-out performance in this large-batch adaptation recipe.

record.problems: Results concern pretrained language-model adaptation on GLUE, not the natural-image and random-label settings in the versions. Main comparisons report accuracy rather than train and test error jointly. Several batch-size sweeps are only described via figures without exact plotted values; no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Figures 1(b), 7, and 8 report trends without recoverable per-condition values; only text-supported aggregate or explicitly stated figure results were retained. Table 5's alternate perturbation-method comparisons are not independent evidence for V5's large-batch penalty and are excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label held-out generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the specified tuning regimes; neither LAMB comparisons nor the Adam ablation supplies this comparison.

Training image classifiers or language models from scratch; language-modeling objectives; normalization changes; a systematic duration sweep establishing when longer training closes the penalty. Results concern pretrained encoders adapted to NLU tasks, with very small datasets excluded.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware weight perturbations, similarly low training losses, train-test generalization gaps, and comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures. Hessian curvature is a different construct.
Removal of highly memorized versus random training examples and retraining.

missing.what: Table 6's learning-rate-scaling comparisons are omitted and not declared in rows_left_out. Record task-level values against small-batch controls: scaled baseline 83.9, 89.2, 90.6/87.4, 92.5; scaled ScaLA 84.9, 90.8, 91.4/88.4, 92.9. Reported averages are 88.7 and 89.7 versus small-batch 89.4. Flag that Table 6 reports 88.5 for the tuned baseline average whereas Table 2 reports 88.4 for identical task values.

LAMB at batch 1K versus small-batch controls is missing. BERT values are 84.1, 89.6, 90.5/87.0, 92.4; RoBERTa values are 90.5, 94.5, 91.3/88.5, 96.2. LAMB leaves penalties on most tasks, with RoBERTa MNLI matching its small-batch control.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source for any version. V5 explicitly allows adapted recipes to remove penalties, so successful recovery does not challenge it. Matching average performance conceals residual task-level penalties. Appendix B specifies six epochs, learning-rate decay and warmup; the 12-epoch comparison is a separate duration experiment. No V7 verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and held-out natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image models and local connectivity.
Generalization comparison of adaptive optimizers and SGD under the version's tuning conditions.

No language-model comparison; no systematic fixed-epoch evaluation of all proposed recipe adaptations such as normalization changes. Results focus on pretrained transformer adaptation to GLUE and include figures whose exact values are not provided.
Dropout intervention and its interaction with training-set size or data augmentation.
Measures largest Hessian eigenvalue as sharpness, but does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or compare it with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal and retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: BERTbase
rows.operation_detail: Compare ScaLA and baseline at batch size 2K over training duration
rows.baseline: baseline has difficulty to reach 84 after training twice longer (12 epochs)
rows.value: ScaLA obtains an accuracy of 85.2 after 6 epochs
rows.note: Text explicitly reports ScaLA's value and baseline's described performance after longer training.
rows.check: Split the duration and recipe comparisons. The baseline still struggles to reach 84 after 12 epochs, below small-batch 84.8; ScaLA reaches 85.2 after six. This qualifies longer training as a remedy here. The supplied text confirms these numbers despite the record's excerpt-verification failure.

source_check.correct: Separate comparisons: ScaLA reaches 85.2 after six epochs at batch 2K, exceeding the six-epoch small-batch reference 84.8, so recipe recovery is observed. The untreated batch-2K baseline has difficulty reaching 84 after 12 epochs; longer training alone does not close the gap.
